messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 75
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Potter
  trauma_type: Refugee
  pcl5: 50

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events, Auditory (Cars): Car sounds, Authority Presence: Police
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Positive Events: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Memory: Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
  Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Low Coping: I can't deal with even the slightest upset, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

Vignette:
Raj’s hands, once so steady, now betrayed him. The lump of grey clay on the wheel, moments from becoming a smooth, symmetrical vase, suddenly faltered and collapsed into a shapeless mound. At 75, he had spent over fifty years at this wheel; it was the one place he had always felt in control. Now, he saw the ruined clay as proof of his own internal collapse, a sign that he was no longer capable of doing the things that had defined him. The frustration felt immense, a tidal wave of despair over something that should have been a simple, muscle-memory task. He was certain he couldn't deal with even the slightest upset anymore. The sound of a truck backfiring on the street outside his small studio sent a jolt through his body, and instantly, he was somewhere else.

It was not a story he could tell, not with a beginning, middle, or end. The memory of fleeing his village as a small boy didn't exist in words. It came in fragmented pieces, sensory snapshots that felt more real and vivid than the sight of his own hands covered in wet clay. There was the frantic grip of his mother’s hand, the smell of dust and sweat from the crowd pressing in on all sides, a blur of khaki uniforms that meant danger, not safety. And there was the sound: a low, constant rumble of engines and shouting that was not about rescue but was part of the chaos itself. When he hears a car engine rev too loudly or sees a police cruiser pass his home, the memory doesn't feel like the past; it feels like it is happening right now, just outside his door. He had come to believe that he had to be especially careful, that you never know what can happen next, a lesson learned in a single, terrifying week nearly seventy years ago.

In the decades that followed, Raj built a new life. He met his wife, Meera, raised a family, and opened his pottery studio, a quiet sanctuary of creation. But the vigilance never left. Over the years, it hardened into a set of unspoken rules. He would find himself at the window multiple times an hour, scanning the quiet suburban street for any sign of threat. Before locking up his studio for the night, he would circle the building twice, checking every window and door, even though his was the only shop on the small, sleepy block. This constant need to check his surroundings was exhausting, but the alternative—the feeling of being unprepared—was unthinkable.

Slowly, his world began to shrink. He started avoiding any situation that might involve disagreement. The slightest elevation in Meera’s voice during a discussion about finances would cause a knot of panic in his stomach, and he would immediately concede, desperate to avoid the confrontation. He learned to placate, to smooth over any ripple of discord, and in doing so, a quiet, hollow space grew between them. He also began to retreat from joy. When their grandson’s fifth birthday party was planned in the local park, Raj developed a sudden, unshakable fatigue. The idea of being in a crowd, of celebrating, of feeling happy or hopeful, felt dangerous, like tempting fate. It was easier to stay home, to keep the world, with its potential for both joy and disaster, at a safe distance.

The breaking point came last month. A dear friend and neighbor of thirty years passed away. The thought of attending the funeral sent Raj into a state of near-paralysis. It was not about mourning his friend; it was about the sight of graves, the formal gathering of grief, which dredged up those nonverbal memories of unburied, unmarked, and countless losses from his childhood. His refusal to go, his inability to even explain why, was a profound hurt to Meera, who had to face their community’s grief alone. Seeing the pain in her eyes, Raj realized that his strategies for survival were now costing him the very life he had worked so hard to build. He came to therapy not with a clear story to tell, but with a collection of fragments and a desperate hope that he might one day be able to sit at his wheel, center the clay, and feel his own hands become steady again.
